messages.author: 53d479b609cc8ad3
messages.subject: -2loglikelihood different between Stan and Monolix.
parts:
Hi,
I ran the same model in Monolix and R software (using rstan) and apprarently they produced different -2loglikelihood.
I have a model based on ODEs which could be stated like:
If t <=2:            dA/dt = -beta*A.
If t>2 and t<=h: dA/dt = gamma*A.
If t>h:               dA/dt = -alpha*A.
Since this system of ODE is quite simple, I can get the analytical form of A (antibody on log10 scale) and formulate the model in rstan where the antibody on log10 scale at time point t has the predicted value of:
If t <=2:                   log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*time)]
If t >2 and t<=h:       log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*2 + gamma*(time-2))]
If t >h:                     log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*2 + gamma*(h-2) -alpha*(time-h))]  
(We use log10 transformation for this typical type of data and have seen its good performance).

I have longitudinal profiles so I fixed non-linear mixed effect model in Monolix with 4 random effects of A0, beta, gamma, alpha. The individual parameters of all four parameters are assumed to have log-normal distribution.
The convergence of this model is well-achieved and we got -2loglikelihood of 462.75.
I fit the same model in Stan where individual parameters of A0 is assumed to have a normal distribution, but for beta, gamma, alpha, it is assumed to have normal distribution (I tried to let these individual parameters to have log-normal distributions as well but the model did not give the good estimate (some parameter estimates are approximately 5.6e207)). However, the -2loglikelihood is -494.114 (I use the mean of the -2loglikelihood).


So one obtained from Monolix is positive and one from Stan is negative.
Does any one have the same problem?
How can we explain for that? Or what am I doing wrong?

I attach the program in the attachment for easy following.
Thank you.

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] -2loglikelihood different between Stan and Monolix.
parts:
Hi. When you refer to the log-likelihood do you mean the one that Stan
calculates, lp__, or the one you calculate in the generated quantities
block, log_lik? lp__ is going to be different because it has the
priors in it (which it doesn't look like you're including in the
calculation of log_lik) and also because of the transformations that
Stan does under the hood, and the fact that constants get dropped.
There's lots of info in the "Transformations of Constrained Variables"
chapter in the manual.

I don't know anything about Monolix...maybe it has default priors? Or
maybe it also drops constants?

Seth

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] -2loglikelihood different between Stan and Monolix.
parts:
Hi Seth,
Thanks for your input.
Actually I meant the loglikelihood that genearted by the generated quantities in Stan.
My model is as below:
model_ex0 <- "
data {
     int<lower=1> N;                         // Total number of data points
     real<lower=0> time[N];                  // Time points
     real<lower=0> y[N];                     // Antibody levels on log10 scale
     int<lower=1>     J;                     // Number of subjects
     int<lower=1, upper=J>    subj[N];       // Subject id
     int<lower=0, upper=1>    cens[N];       // Censoring indication
     int<lower=0, upper=1>    C2[N];         // Child indication
}

parameters {
     real<lower=0> beta;
     real<lower=0> gamma;
     real<lower=4> h;
     real<lower=0> alpha;
     real<lower=0> A0;

     vector[J] b_raw;                          //To apply non-centered parameterization
     vector[J] bbeta;
     vector[J] bgamma;
     vector[J] balpha;


     real<lower=0> sigma_A0;
     real<lower=0> sigma;
     real<lower=0> sigma_beta;
     real<lower=0> sigma_gamma;
     real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;

     real vA0;
     real vbeta;
     real vgamma;
     real valpha;
}

transformed parameters{
     vector[J] b;
     real betapart[N];
     real gammapart[N];
     real alphapart[N];
     real A0part[N];
     real mu[N];
     real diff[N];

     b = sigma_A0*b_raw;
     for (i in 1:N) {
     A0part[i]    = b[subj[i]] +vA0*C2[i];
     betapart[i] = beta + bbeta[subj[i]] + vbeta*C2[i];
     gammapart[i] = gamma + bgamma[subj[i]] +vgamma*C2[i];
     alphapart[i] = alpha  + balpha[subj[i]] +valpha*C2[i]; }

     // The mean
     for (i in 1:N){
        if ( time[i] <= 2 ) {
            mu[i] = log10(A0*exp(A0part[i] -betapart[i]*time[i])) ;  }
        else if ( time[i] >2 && time[i] <=h ) {
            mu[i] = log10(A0*exp(A0part[i] -2*betapart[i] + gammapart[i]*(time[i]-2) ) ) ; }
       else if ( time[i] > h ) {
            mu[i] = log10(A0*exp(A0part[i] - 2*betapart[i] + gammapart[i]*(h-2) -alphapart[i]*(time[i]-h)) );}
     // Calculate (ynew-mu)/sigma and exp(-1/2*(ynew - mu)^2/ sigma^2)
     diff[i] = (y[i] - mu[i])/sigma;
     }

}

model {
     // Priors
     b_raw ~ normal(0, 1);                    //subj random effects - As we apply non-centered parameterization
     bbeta ~ normal(0, sigma_beta);
     bgamma~ normal(0, sigma_gamma);
     balpha~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);
     // Likelihood
     for (i in 1:N){
        if ( cens[i] ==0 ) {
            target += normal_lpdf(y[i] | mu[i], sigma);}
        else if ( cens[i] ==1 ) {
            target += normal_lcdf(y[i] | mu[i], sigma);}
             }
}

generated quantities {
     vector[N] log_lik;
     for (i in 1:N){
        if ( cens[i] ==0 ) {
            log_lik[i] = -log(sqrt(2*pi())) - log(sigma) - (diff[i])^2/2;}
        else if ( cens[i] ==1 ) {
            log_lik[i] = normal_lcdf(diff[i] | 0, 1);}
     }
}
"


Monolix uses Stochastic Approximation Expectation Maximization (SAEM) for estimating the population parameters in context of non-linear mixed effect models.
I have tried the same model in Monolix and SAS (only random A0 as SAS seems not to be able to fit model with 2 random effects or more given the data at hand), and they both gave the close -2loglikelihod: 421.04 and 421.4. In SAS, I use proc nlmixed and the log-likelihood could be written by myself as following:

   if t<= 2 and cens = 0 then
     ll = (1/(sqrt(2*pi*sigma2)))*exp(-(ynew - log10(mu1))**2/ (2*sigma2));
   if t>2 and t <= h and cens = 0 then
     ll = (1/(sqrt(2*pi*sigma2)))*exp(-(ynew - log10(mu2))**2/ (2*sigma2));
   if t > h  and cens = 0 then
     ll = (1/(sqrt(2*pi*sigma2)))*exp(-(ynew - log10(mu3))**2/ (2*sigma2));
   if t<=2 and cens = 1 then
     ll = probnorm((ynew-log10(mu1))/sigma);
   if t>2 and t <=h and cens = 1 then
     ll = probnorm((ynew-log10(mu2))/sigma);
   if t > h and cens = 1 then
     ll = probnorm((ynew-log10(mu3))/sigma);
   L = log(ll); /*Log-likelihood*/

So I believe that these two softwares do not drop the constant.

Thank you.

Thank you Bob.
But I thought that if we used normal_lpdf(diff[i] |0, 1), Stan will drop the constant term which I think it will lead to different results (in terms of comparing -2loglikelihood acorss different software, or in terms of comparing -2loglikelihood of different models). Am I understandig correctly?
For normal_lcdf(diff[i] |0,1): I intend to compute the probability that one observation less than the LOD, and diff[i] = (y[i] - mu[i])/sigma so I think it should be normal_lcdf(diff[i] |0,1).

Thank you for your input of this line: log_lik[i] = cens[i] ? normal_lcdf(diff[i] | 0, 1) : normal_lpdf(diff[i] | 0, sigma);
I will try it with: log_lik[i] = cens[i] ? normal_lcdf(diff[i] | 0 ,1) : ( -log(sqrt(2*pi())) - log(sigma) - (diff[i])^2/2) ;
(Again so that Stan does not drop the constant term log(sqrt(2*pi)))

Thao.

>      real<lower=0> y[N];                     // Antibody levels on log10 scale
>      int<lower=1>     J;                     // Number of subjects
>      int<lower=1, upper=J>    subj[N];       // Subject id
>      int<lower=0, upper=1>    cens[N];       // Censoring indication
>      int<lower=0, upper=1>    C2[N];         // Child indication
> }
>
> parameters {
>      real<lower=0> beta;
>      real<lower=0> gamma;
>      real<lower=4> h;
>      real<lower=0> alpha;
>      real<lower=0> A0;
>
>      vector[J] b_raw;                          //To apply non-centered parameterization
>      vector[J] bbeta;
>      vector[J] bgamma;
>      vector[J] balpha;
>
>
>      real<lower=0> sigma_A0;
>      real<lower=0> sigma;
>      real<lower=0> sigma_beta;
>      real<lower=0> sigma_gamma;
>      real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;
>
>      real vA0;
>      real vbeta;
>      real vgamma;
>      real valpha;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>      vector[J] b;
>      real betapart[N];
>      real gammapart[N];
>      real alphapart[N];
>      real A0part[N];
>      real mu[N];
>      real diff[N];
>
>      b = sigma_A0*b_raw;
>      for (i in 1:N) {
>      A0part[i]    = b[subj[i]] +vA0*C2[i];
>      betapart[i] = beta + bbeta[subj[i]] + vbeta*C2[i];
>      gammapart[i] = gamma + bgamma[subj[i]] +vgamma*C2[i];
>      alphapart[i] = alpha  + balpha[subj[i]] +valpha*C2[i]; }
>
>      // The mean
>      for (i in 1:N){
>         if ( time[i] <= 2 ) {
>             mu[i] = log10(A0*exp(A0part[i] -betapart[i]*time[i])) ;  }
>         else if ( time[i] >2 && time[i] <=h ) {
>             mu[i] = log10(A0*exp(A0part[i] -2*betapart[i] + gammapart[i]*(time[i]-2) ) ) ; }
>        else if ( time[i] > h ) {
>             mu[i] = log10(A0*exp(A0part[i] - 2*betapart[i] + gammapart[i]*(h-2) -alphapart[i]*(time[i]-h)) );}
>      // Calculate (ynew-mu)/sigma and exp(-1/2*(ynew - mu)^2/ sigma^2)
>      diff[i] = (y[i] - mu[i])/sigma;
>      }
>
> }
>
> model {
>      // Priors
>      b_raw ~ normal(0, 1);                    //subj random effects - As we apply non-centered parameterization
>      bbeta ~ normal(0, sigma_beta);
>      bgamma~ normal(0, sigma_gamma);
>      balpha~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);
>      // Likelihood
>      for (i in 1:N){
>         if ( cens[i] ==0 ) {
>             target += normal_lpdf(y[i] | mu[i], sigma);}
>         else if ( cens[i] ==1 ) {
>             target += normal_lcdf(y[i] | mu[i], sigma);}
>              }
> }
>
> generated quantities {
>      vector[N] log_lik;
>      for (i in 1:N){
>         if ( cens[i] ==0 ) {
>             log_lik[i] = -log(sqrt(2*pi())) - log(sigma) - (diff[i])^2/2;}
>         else if ( cens[i] ==1 ) {
>             log_lik[i] = normal_lcdf(diff[i] | 0, 1);}
>      }
> }
> "
>
>
> Monolix uses Stochastic Approximation Expectation Maximization (SAEM) for estimating the population parameters in context of non-linear mixed effect models.
> I have tried the same model in Monolix and SAS (only random A0 as SAS seems not to be able to fit model with 2 random effects or more given the data at hand), and they both gave the close -2loglikelihod: 421.04 and 421.4. In SAS, I use proc nlmixed and the log-likelihood could be written by myself as following:
>
>    if t<= 2 and cens = 0 then
>      ll = (1/(sqrt(2*pi*sigma2)))*exp(-(ynew - log10(mu1))**2/ (2*sigma2));
>    if t>2 and t <= h and cens = 0 then
>      ll = (1/(sqrt(2*pi*sigma2)))*exp(-(ynew - log10(mu2))**2/ (2*sigma2));
>    if t > h  and cens = 0 then
>      ll = (1/(sqrt(2*pi*sigma2)))*exp(-(ynew - log10(mu3))**2/ (2*sigma2));
>    if t<=2 and cens = 1 then
>      ll = probnorm((ynew-log10(mu1))/sigma);
>    if t>2 and t <=h and cens = 1 then
>      ll = probnorm((ynew-log10(mu2))/sigma);
>    if t > h and cens = 1 then
>      ll = probnorm((ynew-log10(mu3))/sigma);
>    L = log(ll); /*Log-likelihood*/
>
> So I believe that these two softwares do not drop the constant.
>
> Thank you.
>
> On Thursday, 15 September 2016 20:29:26 UTC+2, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> Hi. When you refer to the log-likelihood do you mean the one that Stan
> calculates, lp__, or the one you calculate in the generated quantities
> block, log_lik? lp__ is going to be different because it has the
> priors in it (which it doesn't look like you're including in the
> calculation of log_lik) and also because of the transformations that
> Stan does under the hood, and the fact that constants get dropped.
> There's lots of info in the "Transformations of Constrained Variables"
> chapter in the manual.
>
> I don't know anything about Monolix...maybe it has default priors? Or
> maybe it also drops constants?
>
> Seth
>
> On Thu, Sep 15, 2016 at 3:28 PM, Thao Tran <thao...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> > I ran the same model in Monolix and R software (using rstan) and apprarently
> > they produced different -2loglikelihood.
> > I have a model based on ODEs which could be stated like:
> > If t <=2:            dA/dt = -beta*A.
> > If t>2 and t<=h: dA/dt = gamma*A.
> > If t>h:               dA/dt = -alpha*A.
> > Since this system of ODE is quite simple, I can get the analytical form of A
> > (antibody on log10 scale) and formulate the model in rstan where the
> > antibody on log10 scale at time point t has the predicted value of:
> > If t <=2:                   log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*time)]
> > If t >2 and t<=h:       log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*2 +
> > gamma*(time-2))]
> > If t >h:                     log10[A(t)] = log10[A0*exp(-beta*2 +
> > gamma*(h-2) -alpha*(time-h))]
> > (We use log10 transformation for this typical type of data and have seen its
> > good performance).
> >
> > I have longitudinal profiles so I fixed non-linear mixed effect model in
> > Monolix with 4 random effects of A0, beta, gamma, alpha. The individual
> > parameters of all four parameters are assumed to have log-normal
> > distribution.
> > The convergence of this model is well-achieved and we got -2loglikelihood of
> > 462.75.
> > I fit the same model in Stan where individual parameters of A0 is assumed to
> > have a normal distribution, but for beta, gamma, alpha, it is assumed to
> > have normal distribution (I tried to let these individual parameters to have
> > log-normal distributions as well but the model did not give the good
> > estimate (some parameter estimates are approximately 5.6e207)). However, the
> > -2loglikelihood is -494.114 (I use the mean of the -2loglikelihood).
> >
> >
> > So one obtained from Monolix is positive and one from Stan is negative.
> > Does any one have the same problem?
> > How can we explain for that? Or what am I doing wrong?
> >
> > I attach the program in the attachment for easy following.
> > Thank you.
> >
